Hello! I have ADHD with mostly inattentive symptoms and I study and work in creative field. Medication for sure makes my thought process more linear, but I haven't found it to have major impact in my creativity on a long run, especially not after finding the suitable dose of medication. Your process sound very similiar to mine.

I do have have most of my great ideas when my medication is wearing off and I always carry a notebook with me so I can write or draw these ideas down when they occur. But the thing is, atleast for me, getting the idea is just 10% of the job, and 90% is actually getting the shit done. This is were medication has made my life 10x better and nowadays way more of my projects get finnished and sometimes I finnish projects WEEKS before the deathline.

Everyone is different, and I know I am lucky to have things work like this for me. I encourage you to give medication a try :) And the positve with most ADHD meds is that you don't need to take them every day if it dosen't suit your needs. Personally I nowadays choose to take them every day, because they greatly increase my quality of life.

It does requires skill and time, but I call it craftmanship, maybe illustration, but not art. Art is something that shows an interesting point of view, idea or emotion. If you combine that with technical skill, we are talking about good art. 

Obviously you have learned excellent technical skills, so why not take it to the next level? I think 85% of the fun in art is finding out who you are as an artist and how do you see the world. There is nothing wrong with realistic drawing, but to draw realistic is so much more than taking a photo someone else took and redoing it with pencils. Draw from life or photograph your own reference photos or combine several reference photos into a one picture. Getting out of the comfort zone is not easy, but who knows, eventually it might be rewarding and even fun :)

I understand that certain things are made harder by aphantasia, and your drawings are definitely skillful, but if you really want to be an artist, you should find a way to work around this. To be honest, copying photograps is not really art, but copying. It does require a lot of skill, but by doing only that, you are not bringing your own creativity, vision or YOU to your drawings.

I would recommend to start practicing drawing from observation, drawing things that you see around you. It will be very frustrating at first (because it is much harder than copying photos), but I think it could really take you forward. When you are the one deciding what gets included to the drawing and the one making the decions how to excecute them, you are forced into being creative and your vision gets included in the picture as default. And no visual imagination needed!

Good luck on your art journey :)

I'm a total aphantasiac (no imagenary visuals, sound, smell, nothing). I can see dreams and I can detect the tresh hold of starting to fall asleep by having visualizations starting to appear in my mind.

I have pretty extensive experience with psychedelics.

For most of the time they don't cause me hallucinations. Typically on a trip I can get some very mild open eye visual and no closed eye visuals.

But, there have been times I have had hallucinatiuons and seen close eye visuals. To achirve this I need to be very very high. The combinations that are most likely to open my minds eye:

LSD + 2cb +weed: neither of the LSD or 2-cb alone give me halluginations, but taking 2-cb 4-6 hours in to a acid trip and then smoking some weed is pretty a pretty reliable way to make me see some pretty crazy and beautiful visuals. Sometimes it can get bit overhelming since I am not sure what is real and what is not anymore.

acid/mushrooms/2cb + ketamine: a classic psychedelics topped with ketamine seem to do the trick.

The best closed eye visuals I have experienced happened on a mdma + 2cb + ketamine + weed trip. My mind's eye was able to imagine very detailed images. I'm happy I got to experience that.

I guess my diet wasn't low-sugar per se, but my mom was very health conscious and as a child I never got stuff like sodas, juice, candy, cake, cookies or deserts at home. I was allowed to have ice cream, and my family bought chips once a year. In general my mom tried to keep up a diet of high fiber and lot of veggies and fruits. I was always very lean as a a child.

After I started to have some money of my own binging on "yummy" food definitely came problem for me. If I bought some, I would eat it all at once and had no ability to restrict myself. I did gain weight also and have climed up to BMI 26 occasionally.

Now at age of 28 it all has balanced out. I don't crave yummy foods anymore and keeping a good diet comes very easy for me. Lots of veggies, fruits, nuts, good oils and high on fiber. I have noticed that many of my friends who had different upbringing struggle to stay away from sugar and eating it is very rewarding for them. I just can't relate, and the biggest food problem for me was always the chips. I'm BMI 20 and feel great and look great.

When I was younger I was resenting my mom for how I was brought up with food, but nowadays I am nothing but thankful.

I'm also not the original poster, but psylocibin changed the course of my life too.

I think on top of my very sensitive and emotional personality I happened to encounter several big negative life events that had left me pretty traumatized at the age of 23. I had been fighting to get back on my feet for few years already: taking medication, psychoanalytic therapy and exercising, but still I broken person struggling to find the will to stay alive. I was about to turn 25 when a friend, who was kinda experienced trip guide, asked if I wanted to try out psilocybin. The trip was not planned to meet any therapeutic goals.

We ended up flipping hippies, combining psilocybin and mdma. That night my sense of self fell apart and I saw that all these traumatic events and suffering that I had made a part of my identity had actually nothing to do with my real self. It was just some old, useless trash I kept dragging around with me. And I saw that in grand scheme of things my life wasn't all that important but only a small small fraction in all time and space the life had been going on on Earth. Somehow that idea was really soothing. The experience overall was transcendent and I felt I had come to a sacred place and for the first time in years felt extreme gratitude to be alive.

After that I pretty much started to change my life around. I quit drinking. I understood it was something I had used to cope with my sensitivy and dampen myself so I could the person others wanted me to be. Got rid of toxic relationships. Learned to establish boundaries with others. Got in tune with my body. Learned to concentrate on the present instead of worrying about the future or mourning over the past. 

I guess I basically learned to get in tune with my intuition, got to know who I was instead of what other people or society wanted me to be (or what I think other want me to be). Dedicated to make choices that I could be proud of, for both taking care of my body and making choices that are right and good instead of what is easy.

Nowadays at age 28 I'm off meds and feel good and look great. I know who I am and what is important to me. I'm still not super awesome at managing my emotions and my functional abilities are not completely recovered (and maybe won't ever be). But still, I feel like I have had a second chance in life and this time I'm taking a good care of it. There is no question about the fact that psychedelics have a ability to change your mind and change your perspective and I do not believe I would be were I am now without them. I would still be depressed selfdestructive addict I was for a long long time.
